title: The ones with no names
hookLine: strangers sleep in the house the night it burns, and why Hindus say one Self lives in every being
carry: the wise see one self in every being
tomorrow: who is waiting at the river?

cards: The house at Varanavata was made to look like a gift and burn like a torch, with lac, resin and ghee worked into its walls, the text says.
Under its floor is a different secret: a tunnel, dug by a miner Vidura sent, its mouth hidden inside the house. Kunti and her sons are living on top of a fire that hasn't been lit.
Purochana, who built it, lives there too, waiting for his moment. Tonight, someone else strikes first.

teach.h: A FEAST, AND GUESTS WHO STAY.
teach.b: Kunti gives a feast. Brahmins come and eat, and women come, and when it's over the guests go home. But a Nishada woman, of the forest people, has come looking for food with her five sons.
They eat and drink, and fall asleep in the house so heavily, the text says, they're like the dead.
In the dark, Bhima gets up. He sets fire first to where Purochana sleeps, then to the door, then all around the house. The family goes down into the tunnel, and out.
In the morning the townspeople stand at the ashes, grieving. They find Purochana, burned in his own trap. And they find a woman and five young men, and they say: Kunti and her sons are dead.
The text never names them, and doesn't stop to judge the act. But the same epic gives us a way to see them.
Later in the Mahabharata, in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the wise look with an equal eye on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast.
It's called sama-darshana, the equal eye.
Behind it sits one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the same atman, the Self, lives in every being. Nobody is background.

A forest woman the town mistook for a queen, whom the poem never named, carries the same Self as Kunti. The lac house was built to kill the Pandavas. It killed the man who built it, and six people nobody planned for.

how: In Pitru Paksha, the fortnight for the ancestors, many Hindus offer water and sesame, tarpana, for the dead; some tarpana prayers include those who have no relatives to remember them.

games.q: a friend says: they were just extras in the story, so why does it matter who died in the lac house? by today's teaching, what fits?
o: the same Self, atman, lived in them as in Kunti. the wise see every being with an equal eye.
it matters less. they weren't the heroes.
it only matters because their bodies fooled the town.

practice: This one has a cost, so go slowly. If you have water near you, pour a little into a cup.
In Pitru Paksha, many Hindus offer water, tarpana, for the dead, and some of those prayers include people with no family left to remember them.

Bring to mind someone caught up in something that wasn't theirs: a stranger in the news, someone whose name you never learned. Hold them in attention, the way the story doesn't stop to. If you pray, offer the water for them.
If you don't, simply hold them, and know they count.

wordCard.voice: Nishada, a woman of the forest people who slept in the house that night, with her five sons, and was never named.

orig.note: Sanskrit niṣāda: a name for forest-dwelling peoples; the woman who sleeps in the house is a Nishada.

carryVoice: Your line: the wise see one self in every being. Even the ones the story never named. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.
